sections.b: Matthew gathers seven parables into Jesus' third long speech: four told to the crowds from a boat (the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast) and three told to the disciples in the house (the hidden treasure, the pearl, the net). Two are explained in detail (13:18–23, 36–43). Between them Jesus explains why he speaks in parables, quoting Isaiah 6:9–10, and Matthew adds Psalm 78:2. The speech ends with the image of a scribe trained for the kingdom, bringing out new and old things (13:52).

common: The weeds, the treasure, the pearl, the net and the trained scribe are found only in Matthew.

sections.b: Matthew follows Mark's two Sabbath stories but adds arguments: priests work in the temple on the Sabbath without guilt, "here is something greater than the temple" (12:6), and Hosea 6:6, "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice" (12:7). He adds the sheep in a pit (12:11) and the rule "doing good on the Sabbath is allowed" (12:12). Matthew leaves out Mark's saying that the Sabbath was made for people (Mark 2:27). Coming right after Jesus' offer of rest (11:28–30), the stories present Jesus as the one who gives the Sabbath its true meaning.

From prison John sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is "the Coming One." Jesus answers with signs from Isaiah and then praises John as more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1 and Elijah, "the one who was going to come" (11:14). Yet "the smallest one in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he is" (11:11). "This generation" rejected both John, who came fasting, and Jesus, who came eating and drinking (11:18–19).

Many scholars think Matthew presents Jesus as Wisdom in person. "Wisdom is proved right by the things she does" (11:19) follows a list of Jesus' own works (11:2). The Father hides and reveals through the Son (11:25–27), and Jesus calls the weary to take his yoke (11:28–30), as Wisdom invites the simple in Proverbs 9 and Ben Sira calls his students to put their necks under her yoke (Sirach 51:23–27). Others see Jesus here more as Wisdom's messenger.

Jesus invites the worn out and loaded down to come to him and take his yoke, promising "rest for your souls," words from Jeremiah 6:16. The next scenes are set on the Sabbath, the day of rest (12:1–14).

Matthew names four brothers of Jesus and mentions sisters (13:55–56); Mark has "Joses" for Joseph (Mark 6:3). The brothers and Jesus' mother stand outside asking to speak to him in 12:46–50, where Jesus names his disciples as his family. Churches differ on whether these were Mary's children, Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, or cousins; see the card at Matthew 12.

Only Matthew has Jesus say of John, "John himself is Elijah, the one who was going to come" (11:14), applying Malachi 4:5. The saying comes with a condition, "if you are ready to receive it," and Matthew returns to it in 17:10–13. In John 1:21 the Baptist denies being Elijah, which many explain by the difference between being Elijah in person and coming in his role.

Three of Matthew's parables use the farming year: seed that yields thirty, sixty or a hundredfold (13:8, 23), weeds left until the harvest (13:30), and the harvest as "the completion of the age" with angels as reapers (13:39).

sections.h: The Son of Man in Matthew 11–13
sections.b: The title appears in all three settings: the Son of Man who came eating and drinking (11:19), who is Lord of the Sabbath (12:8), who will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (12:40), and who sows the good seed and will send his angels at the end of the age (13:37, 41).
